name: guaymí ngäbere
confidence_why: Lininger Ross 1981 records one unpredictable primary accent per word in Costa Rican Ngäbere (kebé 'shrimp' vs kébe 'termite'), but Abarca González 1985 analyses the same Costa Rican variety as a two-level register tone language with monosyllabic minimal pairs (kei 'tree' vs kéi 'big') and words bearing two high tones, and no later study read (Krohn 2019, Vega Chavarría 2021) settles whether the system is accent or tone.

catalog_quote: El acento primario siempre se manifiesta en palabras monosilábicas. En palabras polisilábicas que no son compuestas, siempre hay un solo acento primario y los demás acentos son secundarios. En estos casos se marca el acento primario en una transcripción fonológica puesto que su posición no es predecible, como se puede comprobar a continuación: (25.) a. / kebé / 'camarón' ... b. / kébe / 'comején' ... A nivel 'ético' en algunas oportunidades el informante ha variado el acento primario de una sílaba a otra optativamente. Con este hecho, su sistema de acento parece tender a llenar el patrón acentual del español, con la regla de colocar el acento primario en la penúltima sílaba de palabras que terminan con una vocal. ... tone_statements.citation: Murillo Miranda, José Manuel. 2008. Notas sobre la lengua guaymí en Costa Rica. Letras (Universidad Nacional, Costa Rica) 43: 75-90. doi:10.15359/rl.1-43.5
tone_statements.quote: Entre estas se encuentran las de Kopesc y Kopesc, Lininger, Arosemena y de Abarca22 , todas las cuales corresponden a estudios fonológicos (principalmente inventarios). El primero establece ocho fonemas vocálicos, dieciocho consonánticos y dos suprasegmentales (acento y nasalización) ; el segundo propone un fonema de labialización /w/ opuesto a un fonema semiconsonántico /w/; Abarca argumenta que el fonema semiconsonántico no es tal, sino alófono de la /uI, además propone que la lengua manifiesta tono alto y tono bajo.
tone_statements.translation: Among these are those of Kopesec & Kopesec, Lininger, Arosemena and Abarca, all of which are phonological studies (mainly inventories). The first establishes eight vowel phonemes, eighteen consonant phonemes and two suprasegmentals (accent and nasalization); the second proposes a labialization phoneme /w/ opposed to a semiconsonant phoneme /w/; Abarca argues that the semiconsonant phoneme is not one but an allophone of /u/, and further proposes that the language displays high tone and low tone.
tone_statements.locator: p.81 (section on previous descriptions), with fn.22 identifying Kopesec & Kopesec 1974, Lininger 1981, Arosemena 1983, Abarca 1985
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Secondhand report only: Kopesec & Kopesec 1974 = contrastive accent (+ nasalization) as the suprasegmentals; Abarca 1985 = two level tones H/L; Murillo takes no position.

tone_statements.citation: Constenla Umaña, Adolfo. 1991. Las lenguas del área intermedia: introducción a su estudio areal. San José: Editorial de la Universidad de Costa Rica. 216 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Quesada Pacheco (2008) does not find tone in Guaymí to be contrastive at present, but this does not exclude the possibility that the language or some dialects had phonemic tone in the past (ibid.: 42). In fact, Abarca (1985: 18), cited in Quesada Pacheco (2008: 42), identifies high and low tone in Guaymí, for instance in /tù/ ‘tooth’, /kɾì/ ‘tree’, /kɾí/ ‘tall’, and /kɔ̀/ ‘name’. These tones are not reproduced in the present work … since the existence of lexical tone in the terms in question was not corroborated by the consultants in his study (ibid.: 42).
tone_statements.locator: p. 371, sec. 2.3.13.1.1 'Guaymí vowels and suprasegmentals'; cf. also p. 514, sec. 2.4.1.5 'Stress and tone'
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Following Quesada Pacheco 2008, tone is not contrastive in present-day Guaymí; Abarca's 1985 high/low tones were not confirmed by consultants; some dialects may have lexical tone. Stress is phonemic.

readall_conflicts: The only listed work (Kopesec & Kopesec 1974) could not be opened, so no first-hand conflict can be stated. Secondhand, Abarca González 1985 (ELCh 4, p. 35, already held by the project from the earlier reading) reports that the SIL (Instituto Lingüístico de Verano) researchers and Barbara Lininger analysed Guaymí Movere as having accent (stress), while Abarca herself analyses the Costa Rican Movere variety as a two-level register tone language (high vs low; her section 1.1.3 'Fonemas tonales', PDF page 7: 'El guaymí movere presenta un sistema tonal de registro integrado por dos niveles: alto y bajo'). Later Panamanian acoustic/phonotactic papers held by the project (Krohn 2019 Káñina; Vega Chavarría 2021 Letras; the two Amelica/Redes papers) speak of 'sílaba acentuada / posición con respecto al acento' as a conditioning factor for consonant lenition and vowel quality but give no placement rule, and one of them notes secondhand that Ngäbere is described as tonal.

audit.recode_to: Pending Quesada Pacheco 2008 / Murillo 2016: at minimum add contra = Abarca 1985 (two-register tone; rejects Lininger's accent analysis; Constenla concurs) and a caution that the Panamanian dialect is reported non-tonal (Quesada Pacheco 2006 n.11). If the modern grammars side with Abarca/Constenla for the CR variety, reclassify kind from 'lexical' (stress) to tone / no-contrastive-stress; if Quesada Pacheco 2008 gives a stress rule for Panama, code that and flag the dialect split.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim in the Lininger 1981 text we hold at p.109 §C.1.b and p.110. (2) The deciding source is a 1981 15-page tagmemic phonology sketch from one Costa Rican informant whose own text flags tonal 'vestiges' and optional accent shifting; Glottolog lists a 2008 Lincom reference grammar (xi+190) and web search finds a 2016 grammar of the CR dialect with a phonology chapter, neither held, both print-only.
